topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health contexts; competency frameworks may have limited direct applicability to Australian workplace settings or non-public-health sectors, though core digital literacy principles may transfer.
takeaways: Review identifies specific digital competencies required in public health roles — use this as a reference point to map which competencies are most critical in your organisation's AI-adjacent roles.

Scoping reviews synthesise existing frameworks rather than test new approaches; consider whether the European frameworks identified align with Australian regulatory, ethical, or professional standards in your sector.
The updated scope suggests digital competency requirements are evolving — useful for identifying skill gaps that may emerge as AI tools proliferate in your industry.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears focused on public health faculty contexts; generalisability to other sectors and non-academic settings unclear from snippet alone.
takeaways: Faculty development programmes can shift mindsets from AI resistance to readiness; consider designing structured learning pathways that address concerns and build confidence before expecting workforce adoption.
Public health organisations can use faculty/leader upskilling as a lever to drive broader AI literacy — investing in key influencers' capabilities may have cascading effects across teams.
Framing AI literacy development as a change management challenge (moving from resistance to readiness) rather than purely technical training may increase engagement and sustainability.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis draws on global consulting experience but findings reflect perspectives of large multinational organisations that typically have greater resources for AI transformation than SMEs.
takeaways: AI adoption requires simultaneous workforce planning: identify skill gaps early, design reskilling pathways, and align hiring with AI implementation timelines rather than treating workforce changes as an afterthought.
Create clear role transitions for existing employees—define which roles will evolve, which will be eliminated, and which are new—to reduce uncertainty and maintain engagement during AI rollout.

Combine technical AI literacy with soft skills training (change management, data thinking, collaboration with AI systems) since technical knowledge alone does not ensure effective adoption or employee buy-in.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development requires translation and adaptation.
takeaways: A holistic digital literacy framework integrating AI competencies should address multiple dimensions (technical, ethical, social) rather than treating AI as an isolated skill — consider how your organisation's AI literacy programmes connect AI learning to broader digital citizenship and responsible technology use.

Middle school frameworks may inform adult onboarding by showing how foundational AI concepts (how AI works, bias, data literacy) should precede advanced technical skills — audit your current AI training sequencing to ensure employees have solid conceptual foundations before role-specific applications.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context; applicability to corporate and other sectors requires validation. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet.
takeaways: AI literacy functions as a foundational meta-skill that integrates technical, critical thinking, ethical, and adaptive domains — consider mapping these four domains when designing AI capability programmes for your workforce.

In higher education settings, positioning AI literacy as a meta-skill (rather than a standalone technical competency) may help staff see how AI capability connects to their existing management and academic roles.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context, which may not directly transfer to corporate workforce development. Specific institutional approaches may vary by country and university type.
takeaways: Integrate AI literacy across multiple disciplines rather than siloing it in computer science; this builds broader competency in your organisation's diverse teams.
Combine theoretical knowledge with hands-on, project-based learning; employees develop AI capabilities more effectively when they can apply concepts to real work problems.
Create structured progression pathways from foundational AI literacy to intermediate and advanced competencies, allowing staff to build skills incrementally alongside their existing roles.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — depends on sample size, industry sectors included, and geographic scope of participating organisations. The 'double-edged' framing suggests the study found both positive and negative effects, which may vary by implementation context.
takeaways: AI adoption creates paradoxical effects on creativity: assess your organisation's current implementation to identify which mechanism is dominant (enhancement vs. constraint) so you can design interventions to amplify benefits and mitigate risks.

Monitor for creativity suppression pathways — the research suggests AI can reduce creative thinking in some contexts; evaluate whether your team's creativity has shifted since AI rollout and adjust task design or autonomy levels accordingly.

Design AI integration to preserve employee agency in creative work — the 'double-edged' finding implies that passive AI dependency may harm creativity while complementary AI use preserves it; tailor adoption strategy accordingly.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to paternalistic leadership contexts, which are more prevalent in collectivist cultures (particularly East Asia). Generalisability to Western individualistic organisations with different leadership styles is limited.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in customizing or 'crafting' how AI is implemented and used in their roles — this enhances collaboration and adoption more than top-down deployment.

In paternalistic leadership environments, leaders should emphasize care and mentorship while guiding AI adoption, as this combination strengthens employees' sense of ownership and willingness to engage with new technologies.

AI crafting (allowing employees agency in shaping AI workflows) acts as a mechanism linking psychological ownership to collaboration — consider designing implementation processes that give teams input into AI tool configuration and use cases.

articles.title: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — APA-published perspective on AI and cognition likely reflects US psychological research and academic contexts; applicability to Australian workplace settings would depend on the specific claims and evidence presented in the full article.
takeaways: AI adoption may create pressure to develop meta-cognitive skills — the ability to monitor and manage your own thinking and learning — which organisations can support through reflective practice and feedback mechanisms.

Understanding how AI reshapes cognitive demands can inform targeted upskilling: identify which human skills (e.g. critical evaluation, creativity, interpersonal reasoning) remain uniquely valuable and design development programs accordingly rather than generic 'AI literacy'.

Psychological frameworks on skill adaptation suggest change readiness varies by individual; assess employee concerns about AI's impact on their thinking and role to surface resistance early and tailor communication strategies.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone; geographic scope, sample size, and sector characteristics are not provided.
takeaways: Role ambiguity—unclear expectations about how to use AI in your job—can impede effective employee-AI collaboration; clarifying AI responsibilities and decision-making boundaries with your team can improve adoption.

Self-efficacy (confidence in your ability to use AI effectively) appears to be a key factor in determining whether employees successfully integrate generative AI into their work; targeted training and early wins can build this confidence.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing contexts and may not generalise to other professions or healthcare roles. The three-wave design strengthens causal inference, but sector-specific nature limits application beyond healthcare settings.
takeaways: Work autonomy is a critical psychological mechanism: employees who maintain control over their tasks when adopting medical AI systems report better wellbeing — design implementation strategies that preserve (rather than restrict) clinician decision-making authority.

AI readiness alone doesn't guarantee positive outcomes — pairing technical training with attention to job design and autonomy is essential to prevent burnout and disengagement among frontline staff adopting new AI tools.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings; while worker uncertainty regarding AI is a global phenomenon, this report reflects American labour market conditions, workplace norms, and policy context that may differ significantly in Australia.
takeaways: Acknowledge and normalise uncertainty about AI's impact on roles — employees experiencing anxiety about job security and skill relevance need explicit reassurance and transparent communication about how AI will be used in your organisation.

Proactively map which tasks AI will augment (not replace) and involve employees in identifying how their work will change — this reduces ambiguity and helps people see themselves as adaptive rather than threatened.
Create structured opportunities for psychological safety conversations: invite employees to voice concerns about automation, competence, and career progression without fear of stigma or consequences.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on Deloitte's consulting experience across clients, but lacks transparent methodology, sample details, or peer review. Findings likely reflect practices in large, well-resourced organisations and may not transfer to smaller or resource-constrained settings.
takeaways: Shift from 'AI adoption' (technology deployment) to 'AI adaptation' (behaviour change) as your framing—this reorients change initiatives toward building employee capability and confidence rather than just rolling out tools.

Design change programmes that explicitly target the human behaviours needed for AI use (e.g. comfort with ambiguity, collaborative problem-solving with AI), not just the technical training—this increases sustained engagement and reduces resistance.
Use a phased, feedback-driven approach that tests and refines the behaviours you want to see, rather than a one-off 'train and deploy' model.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The theoretical framework (cognitive appraisal of stress and Job Demands-Resources) is robust, but geographic scope, sector, sample size, and cultural context are unclear from the information provided.
takeaways: AI awareness can influence how employees reshape their roles through two distinct pathways — understand whether your team members are appraising AI as a threat (stress response) or opportunity (resource), as this determines how they'll engage in job crafting.

Use the Job Demands-Resources framework to diagnose whether your organisation is inadvertently increasing job demands without adequate resources when introducing AI — employees who feel overwhelmed may disengage from proactive role redesign.

Design interventions that reframe AI awareness positively — employees who cognitively appraise AI as manageable are more likely to proactively craft their roles, whereas those experiencing stress-based appraisal may need additional support or role clarity first.

articles.title: Using the behavior change wheel (BCW) framework for health interventions focusing on diet and physical activity in the workplace: a scoping review - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Using the behavior change wheel (BCW) framework for health interventions focusing on diet and physical activity in the workplace: a scoping review  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — scoping review of BCW applications in workplace health interventions across multiple studies, but findings depend on the quality and diversity of included studies; applicability may vary by workplace context and cultural setting.
takeaways: The BCW framework systematically maps behaviour change interventions by linking specific behaviours to intervention functions (education, incentivisation, coercion, etc.) and policy categories — use this structured approach to diagnose which levers are most relevant before designing your workplace wellness programme.

Workplace diet and physical activity interventions often succeed when they address capability (skills and knowledge), opportunity (environmental and social cues), and motivation (habits and goals) together — avoid single-tactic interventions and audit all three domains in your current approach.

Document which BCW components are under-used in your organisation (e.g. environmental restructuring, social support) and test implementation of neglected levers as a way to strengthen existing initiatives without starting from scratch.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford business school perspective without detailed empirical data or geographic scope specified. Findings may reflect developed-economy contexts and higher-education sector biases.
takeaways: Identify specific roles in your organisation where AI augmentation (rather than replacement) could expand employee capabilities — map these systematically before implementing change initiatives.

Design transition support that addresses both technical skilling and psychological readiness, as employees' willingness to adopt AI depends on perceiving it as enhancing rather than threatening their role.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry observations across sectors, but specific implementation details and timelines may vary by organisation size, industry, and existing AI maturity.
takeaways: Identify which of the three horizons (immediate wins, scaling capabilities, transformative impact) your organisation currently operates in, then design behaviour change interventions that match the maturity level and investment horizon of each phase.

Structure AI adoption as a staged journey rather than a single change event — use the three-horizon framework to set realistic expectations with stakeholders and align incentives across short-term adoption and long-term capability building.

Map employee upskilling and culture-change activities to each horizon: horizon one requires quick wins to build confidence; horizon two needs sustained capability development; horizon three demands strategic mindset shifts — tailor your messaging and support accordingly.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's perspective draws on consulting experience across sectors and geographies, but specific findings and recommendations may reflect practices most relevant to large, well-resourced organisations in developed economies.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology rollout — prioritise identifying which roles will change, which skills become critical, and which teams need upskilling first.

Design change management interventions that address both technical reskilling and mindset shifts; resistance to AI often stems from uncertainty about job security and role value, not technical complexity.
Establish clear career pathways and redeployment plans early in the transformation to build trust and reduce defensive behaviours that slow adoption.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from snippet — likely a single study, but geographic location and sample characteristics not specified. Findings may not generalise beyond the specific population studied.
takeaways: People high in antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, combative traits) may have a surprising romantic advantage in initial attraction — counterintuitive because we typically assume narcissism repels partners.
The finding highlights a gap between short-term romantic appeal and long-term relationship quality — traits that attract initially often damage relationships over time.

This research illustrates why evolutionary and psychological mechanisms sometimes favour traits we consciously dislike: antagonistic confidence and boldness can signal status or genetic fitness in ways that trigger attraction despite red flags.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and size, which are not detailed in the snippet provided. Results may be limited to the specific population studied.
takeaways: People with different personality traits remember surprising events in distinctly different ways — some personalities 'lock in' unexpected moments more vividly than others.
This finding suggests that eyewitness accounts of the same surprising event could vary wildly between people not just because of where they were standing, but because of who they fundamentally are.
If you've ever wondered why you and a friend remember the same wild moment completely differently, your personality type might be doing more heavy lifting than you thought.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline sensationalism obscures the actual research basis. Without access to the underlying study details, generalisability cannot be assessed, but neuroimaging findings on psychopathy typically come from small, clinical samples that may not represent the general population.
takeaways: Brain imaging research on psychopathy consistently finds structural and functional differences in regions associated with emotion processing and decision-making — counterintuitively, these aren't simply 'broken' brains but show different patterns of neural organisation.

The term 'shocking difference' is clickbait — neuroscience findings on psychopathy are rarely as clear-cut as headlines suggest, and brain differences don't determine behaviour in a simple cause-and-effect way.
Psychopathy exists on a spectrum in the general population, not as a binary trait, which makes neuroscience findings more nuanced and less 'shocking' than sensationalised media coverage implies.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — full methodology and sample details would be needed to assess generalisability of wine-review–personality associations.
takeaways: AI can detect personality traits from writing style in unexpected places — wine reviews apparently reveal whether someone is conscientious, open, or agreeable, suggesting our taste descriptions leak personal psychology.
The finding is pleasantly quirky: what you say about a Pinot Noir or Chardonnay may tell a psychologist more about you than about the wine itself.

It highlights how machine learning finds patterns in 'throwaway' text that humans might miss, opening the door to personality assessment through everyday writing (though the practical limits of this approach remain worth questioning).

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on twin study methodology and sample composition, which are not detailed in the snippet provided. Twin studies typically assume equal environments for identical and fraternal twins, an assumption that may not always hold.
takeaways: Authoritarian political beliefs have a genetic component — this challenges the common assumption that such views are purely learned or environmentally shaped.
The 'nature vs nurture' split for political ideology isn't clean; both genetic predisposition and environment play surprising roles in shaping how people relate to authority.

What makes this finding counterintuitive: many people assume their political views are entirely rational choices, yet twin studies suggest underlying heritable traits influence susceptibility to authoritarian thinking.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone, but given the critical framing of the question, findings likely apply broadly to MBTI's general validity across diverse populations and organizational contexts.
takeaways: The MBTI is surprisingly poor at predicting actual leadership behaviors — a finding that contradicts its widespread use in corporate leadership development programs worldwide.

Despite decades of popularity in business, the evidence suggests MBTI personality types don't reliably forecast who will be an effective leader, making it an interesting case study in how intuitive-sounding tools can persist without strong scientific support.

This research highlights the gap between what organizations *believe* about personality assessment and what the data actually shows — a fascinating quirk of workplace psychology that affects millions of people taking the test annually.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics, which are not detailed in the snippet. The focus on leader power distance orientation suggests potential applicability across cultures, but limitations would depend on whether the sample is single-country or multi-country.
takeaways: Inclusive leadership directly strengthens team psychological safety, which then drives innovation outcomes — consider auditing your leadership communication for inclusive behaviours (inviting input, acknowledging diverse perspectives) as a lever for both safety and creative problem-solving.

Leader power distance orientation (hierarchy preference) moderates this relationship — leaders who hold strong hierarchical views may inadvertently undermine psychological safety even when practising inclusive behaviours, so self-awareness of power dynamics is critical to making inclusivity efforts effective.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings are specific to multicultural academic team contexts and may not generalise to corporate or other organisational settings. Geographic scope unclear from snippet provided.
takeaways: AI-assisted tools can support inclusive leadership practices in diverse teams, but their effectiveness depends on how leaders implement them — consider piloting AI-facilitated feedback or decision-making processes to reduce unconscious bias in hiring, promotion, or task allocation.

Monitor for unintended gender-related outcomes when introducing AI tools in team leadership — establish baseline metrics on representation and psychological safety before and after implementation to ensure technology reduces rather than reinforces existing inequities.

Inclusive leadership with AI support may require explicit training for leaders on how to interpret and act on algorithmic recommendations; passive reliance on AI alone risks reproducing systemic biases rather than mitigating them.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad — PwC's global workforce survey typically covers multiple countries and sectors, though specific sample characteristics (size, industries, respondent demographics) are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Use survey findings to identify which psychological safety concerns are most prevalent across your workforce — this can help prioritise interventions addressing the fears most impacting your team's engagement and willingness to speak up.

Compare your organisation's psychological safety baseline against global benchmarks from this survey to understand whether your challenges are sector-specific, geography-specific, or broadly shared — informing whether solutions need local customisation.

Map hopes and fears to specific team dynamics: employees worried about job security or AI displacement may be less likely to raise concerns or experiment; consider how transparent communication about change can reduce fear-driven silence.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full study methods — the snippet does not specify sample size, geography, sectors studied, or whether findings are correlational or causal. Readers should review the full methodology to assess applicability to their context.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent investment in psychological safety and ethical leadership may increase employee depression risk; proactively establish clear ethical AI frameworks and create safe spaces for employees to voice concerns about AI implementation.

Psychological safety acts as a protective factor in AI transitions — teams that feel safe speaking up about AI-related anxieties and challenges are less likely to experience negative mental health outcomes, so foster an environment where employees can openly discuss AI fears without penalty.

Ethical leadership matters during AI adoption; leaders who model ethical decision-making and transparency about AI's limitations and risks help employees feel more secure and less anxious about technological change.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but without access to the full article, sample characteristics and methodological rigor cannot be assessed. Findings may reflect BCG's client base rather than broader populations.
takeaways: Create explicit norms and leader behaviours that welcome diverse perspectives and questions — psychological safety removes barriers that prevent quieter or junior employees from contributing equally, directly improving idea generation and problem-solving.

Measure psychological safety through confidential team surveys or pulse checks to identify where trust gaps exist, then address them through transparent communication about mistakes and inclusive decision-making practices rather than top-down solutions.

articles.title: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams - Deloitte
articles.snippet: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Deloitte perspective piece without disclosed sample details, geographic scope, or methodology. Findings may reflect consulting firm observations rather than empirical research, limiting generalisation to specific organisational contexts.
takeaways: Identify and assess the human capabilities (e.g., communication, trust, adaptability) that distinguish high-performing teams in your organisation, then design targeted development interventions around capability gaps rather than assuming generic team-building approaches will work.

Create explicit team norms and structures that prioritise psychological safety by ensuring human capabilities like voice, vulnerability, and collaborative problem-solving are valued and rewarded in performance metrics and team rituals.
